en.name: Denis of Paris
en.summary: Third-century missionary bishop sent to evangelize Roman Gaul, martyred by beheading and said to have carried his own severed head afterward.
en.body: Denis was a missionary bishop sent from Rome to evangelize the Roman province of Gaul in the third century, establishing a Christian community in Lutetia, the settlement that would grow into Paris, at a time when the region remained overwhelmingly pagan and any organized missionary activity carried real risk. He was arrested along with two companions, a priest and a deacon, during a local persecution and, according to a widely repeated medieval tradition, was beheaded on the hill later named Montmartre, meaning "Mount of Martyrs" in his honor, and the legend holds that after his execution he picked up his own severed head and walked several miles while preaching a sermon before finally collapsing at the spot where he was buried. The abbey and later great Gothic cathedral built over his tomb, the Basilica of Saint-Denis, became the traditional burial site of the kings of France for over a thousand years, making him one of the most historically significant patron saints of the French monarchy and of Paris itself.
